study summary / 006

What does one hour in the forest do to the brain?

A randomized Berlin experiment compares forest and busy-street walks.

One hour among trees. One hour along a busy shopping street. I often ask myself whether the brain feels the difference after a walk. An experiment in Berlin sent people on one of these two walks and looked at their brains before and after.

The study

63 healthy adults were randomly assigned to a forest walk or a walk along a busy Berlin shopping street. Functional MRI before and after included a faces task and a social stress task.

The findings

Amygdala activity during the faces task decreased after the forest walk and remained stable after the urban walk. The social stress task also showed a group-by-time interaction, but its forest-only decrease was not statistically significant. Self-reported stress, cognition and physiological stress measures showed no significant group-by-time interactions.

Architectural interpretation

For me, the way to the forest is architecture too. A path, the edge of a park, a green route through the city: these are design decisions. This study tested one walk in one forest, nothing more. It did not test the view from a window or a tree in a courtyard, and it does not show that the street harmed anyone. It tells me that access to nature belongs in the plan, and that its effect deserves to be measured.

Limits and conclusion

This small experiment concerns short-term functional activity, not lasting structural change or disease prevention. It provides evidence for the tested forest walk, while the unchanged urban response should not be described as harm from the city.

original study

Sudimac, Sale & Kühn (2022)
How nature nurtures: Amygdala activity decreases as the result of a one-hour walk in nature. Molecular Psychiatry, 27(11), 4446-4452.

doi: 10.1038/s41380-022-01720-6
